performers: Léner String Quartet: Jenö Léner and Joszef Smilovits, violins; Sándor Roth, viola; Imre Hartman, cello
intro: The Léner Quartet play Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 14 in C♯ minor, Op. 131, complete in its seven linked movements. A solo violin begins, and a dance, a song shared among the four players and a Presto played close to the bridge come before the final C♯ major chords.

sections.label: A · Fugue in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: C♯ minor; the four instruments enter one by one.

sections.label: B · Allegro molto vivace in D major
sections.mNote: Allegro molto vivace; a violin tune in 6/8.

sections.label: Link · Eleven bars of recitative
sections.mNote: Short phrases pass from player to player.

sections.label: Theme · A major theme shared by two violins
sections.mNote: A major theme and variations; the cello plays pizzicato at the start.

sections.label: C · Presto in E major, cello first
sections.mNote: E major; quick notes, sudden rests, bowing near the bridge.

sections.label: D · Adagio, G♯ minor, viola opening
sections.mNote: Twenty-eight slow bars in G♯ minor.

sections.label: E · C♯ minor, then major close
sections.mNote: Allegro; the four players attack together.

cues.title: Opening fugue, first violin
cues.text: The first violin begins a slow fugue in C♯ minor, marked Adagio ma non troppo e molto espressivo. The other three instruments enter in turn with the subject while the earlier voices continue. The cello has a melody of its own.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 6 No. 50, Breitkopf & Härtel, 1863, printed p. 119: Adagio ma non troppo e molto espressivo and four successive fugal entries. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus131.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Conversation books, December 1825
cues.text: Around 11 December 1825 Beethoven wrote the fugue subject into a conversation book. In January 1826, with rehearsals for Op. 130 under way, his friend Karl Holz suggested trying something of the C♯ minor quartet too, and asked whether the first piece was already finished.
cues.evidence: Creation of the work, including the fugue subject in a conversation book around 11 December 1825 and Holz’s question in January 1826 (Beethoven conversation books, BKh 8, p. 273): https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/

cues.title: Léner Quartet recording, London, 1924
cues.text: The Léner Quartet recorded the work in 1924 at Columbia’s Petty France studios in London. The fugue was recorded on 11 February, and the variations and most of the later movements on 21 and 22 February. The dance and the recitative followed on 25 August.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Columbia M-6 (matrices AX300–AX332, dated 11, 21, 22 February and 25 August 1924): https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/595384. Studio and side-by-side layout: https://archive.org/details/l-1581-5-beethoven-quartet-op-131

cues.title: Beethoven and Karl Holz
cues.text: “My dearest friend, I have had another idea,” Beethoven told Karl Holz, second violin of the Schuppanzigh Quartet. He also told Holz that he thought this his best quartet.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus Bonn, exhibition guide “The string quartets of Beethoven”, showcase 1 (text by Michael Ladenburger): https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf

cues.title: Wagner on the opening fugue, 1870
cues.text: Writing in 1870, Richard Wagner called this opening movement one “than which probably nothing more melancholy has been expressed in tones”. He described it as the awakening on the morning of a day that would grant not one wish.
cues.evidence: Richard Wagner, Beethoven (1870), trans. Edward Dannreuther (London: William Reeves, 1903 printing), p. 62, on “his great string-quartet in C-sharp minor”: https://archive.org/details/beethoven1903wagn

cues.title: Schubert’s last illness, November 1828
cues.text: In November 1828, during his last illness, Schubert asked to hear this quartet, and Holz’s quartet played it for him. Holz recalled that “Schubert was sent into such transports of delight and enthusiasm and was so overcome that we all feared for him.”
cues.evidence: Karl Holz’s recollection, printed in Otto Erich Deutsch, Schubert: Memoirs by His Friends (London: A. & C. Black, 1958), and quoted in Christopher H. Gibbs, The Life of Schubert (Cambridge University Press, 2000), who credits it to Ludwig Nohl.

cues.title: Dedication to Stutterheim, 1827
cues.text: In March 1827 Beethoven asked Schott to put Baron Joseph von Stutterheim’s name on the quartet. Stutterheim had accepted Beethoven’s nephew Karl into his regiment.
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Schott, 10 March 1827, BGA 2278; dedication and Stutterheim’s connection to Karl documented at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/ and in the Beethoven-Haus quartet exhibition guide, p. 11.

cues.title: Move from C♯ to D major
cues.text: The fugue ends with all four instruments on C♯. The next movement, an Allegro molto vivace in 6/8, rises a semitone to D major. The first violin plays the tune, accompanied by the other three.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 122: held C♯ octaves, then D-major Allegro molto vivace in 6/8.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Attacca instruction and retuning
cues.text: Beethoven marked the seven pieces to be played without a break. The musicians asked when they would have the chance to retune their instruments.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus Bonn, exhibition guide “The string quartets of Beethoven”, showcase 1 (text by Michael Ladenburger): the attacca instruction and the players’ question about retuning. https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf

cues.title: Columbia issue, November 1924
cues.text: Columbia issued the quartet in November 1924 on five double-sided discs, as L 1581–1585 in Britain and as Masterworks Set No. 6 in the United States. Side 3 held the dance and the recitative together. Side 7 held the end of the variations and the start of the Presto.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive item description (British issue L 1581–1585, US 67021-D–67025-D, side-by-side contents of each side): https://archive.org/details/l-1581-5-beethoven-quartet-op-131. Matrix dates: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/595384

cues.title: Third movement, eleven bars
cues.text: The dance ends and short, speech-like phrases follow. They pass down through the quartet before the first violin plays running notes above held chords. The movement is eleven bars long and leads into the next.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 126–127, complete third movement; eleven-bar length confirmed in the Beethoven-Haus guide, p. 11: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variation theme, two violins
cues.text: The two violins share a melody in A major, one continuing where the other stops. The viola holds a quieter line between them, and the cello plays the accompaniment pizzicato. This theme opens the quartet’s longest movement, a set of variations.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 127: Andante ma non troppo e molto cantabile, 2/4, divided violin melody and pizzicato cello. Variations continue through p. 137.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Publication in parts, 1827
cues.text: Schott published the quartet in parts in May and June 1827, first in Paris and then in Mainz. Beethoven had died in March, and the first players read from single parts. The full score followed in February 1828.
cues.evidence: Creation and publication: Schott edition in parts, May/June 1827; full score February 1828; Beethoven’s death on 26 March 1827 (sixteen days after his letter of 10 March). https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/

cues.title: Announced as Op. 129, April 1827
cues.text: In April 1827 Schott announced the quartet as Op. 129. Artaria’s Op. 130 had not yet appeared, and the publishers’ numbering had gone wrong. On 27 April Artaria corrected the sequence, and the C♯ minor quartet was registered as Op. 131.
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Schott, 22 February 1827 (BGA 2262); Artaria to Schott, 27 April 1827; correspondence of Schindler with the publishers: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/

cues.title: Engraver’s copy for Schott, 1826
cues.text: Schott asked whether the quartet was new. In August 1826 Beethoven sent the engraver’s copy with a joke written on it: “Stolen together from this and that.” He then had to assure the publisher that the music was brand new.
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s inscription on the engraver’s copy sent to Schott in August 1826, “Nb: zusammengestohlen aus verschiedenem diesem u. jenem”; our translation. Subsequent explanatory letter BGA 2187: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/.

cues.title: Dedication to Wolfmayer, 1827
cues.text: On 22 February 1827 Beethoven told Schott that the quartet was for his friend Johann Nepomuk Wolfmayer. On 10 March he wrote again, begging Schott “by everything in the world” to change the dedication if it had already been engraved. Wolfmayer later received Op. 135.
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Schott, 22 February 1827 (BGA 2262) and 10 March 1827 (“so bitte ich Sie um alles in der Welt, dieß abzuändern”; our translation). https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/

cues.title: Engraver’s copy in Bonn
cues.text: The copyist’s manuscript that Beethoven corrected and sent to Schott spent 177 years elsewhere before it reached the Beethoven-Haus in Bonn, with help from the violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter. Its cover page carries corrections in Beethoven’s own hand.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus Bonn, exhibition guide “The string quartets of Beethoven”, showcase 1 on Op. 131 (text by Michael Ladenburger): https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf

cues.title: Schumann on this quartet and Op. 127
cues.text: Robert Schumann wrote that this quartet and Op. 127 seemed to him to stand, with some of Bach’s choruses and organ pieces, “on the extreme boundary of all that has hitherto been attained by human art and imagination”.
cues.evidence: Robert Schumann, “A Retrospective View”, in Music and Musicians: Essays and Criticisms, trans. Fanny Raymond Ritter (London, 1877), p. 391: https://archive.org/details/musicandmusicia00schugoog

cues.title: Opening of the Presto, cello
cues.text: A short cello figure opens the E major Presto. The other three players enter with clipped notes, and rests break up the phrases. Later Beethoven asks for sul ponticello — bowing close to the bridge — which gives the same strings a thin, metallic edge.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 138, cello opening and rests; p. 147, sul ponticello. The effect is discussed in the Beethoven-Haus quartet exhibition guide, p. 11.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Performances in the first fifty years
cues.text: In its first fifty years the quartet was played 260 times. Op. 130 reached 214 performances over the same period, and Op. 132 reached 274.
cues.evidence: Performance counts for the first fifty years after publication: Beethoven-Haus Bonn, exhibition guide “The string quartets of Beethoven”, showcase 8. https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf

cues.title: Sul ponticello near the end of the Presto
cues.text: Near the end of the Presto all four players bow sul ponticello, close to the bridge, at pianissimo. A museum exhibition guide calls the instruction unique and the sound thin, metallic and uncanny. A marked return to ordinary bowing leads to a loud close.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 6 No. 50, Breitkopf & Härtel, printed p. 147 (last page of the Presto): sul ponticello in all four parts, pp and sempre pp, then “da capo per l’ordinario”, a loud close and attacca. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus131.pdf. Beethoven-Haus Bonn, exhibition guide, showcase 1: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sixth movement, Adagio
cues.text: The viola begins a slow G♯ minor melody in 3/4. The sixth movement, Adagio quasi un poco andante, lasts twenty-eight bars, and a first-violin flourish leads into the finale.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 148, complete sixth movement: Adagio quasi un poco andante, 3/4, viola opening and connecting violin flourish. Length confirmed by Beethoven-Haus, p. 11.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Finale, Allegro in C♯ minor
cues.text: The finale, an Allegro in cut time, returns to C♯ minor. All four players play the opening figures together. The first violin then takes the melody above an offbeat accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 148–150: Allegro in cut time, coordinated opening figures and first-violin melody against offbeat accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First public performance, Halberstadt, 1828
cues.text: The first public performance took place in Halberstadt on 5 June 1828, more than a year after Beethoven’s death. Müller organised it.
cues.evidence: First public performance, 5 June 1828, organised by Müller in Halberstadt: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/

cues.title: Arnold Schering’s Hamlet reading
cues.text: The musicologist Arnold Schering heard Hamlet in this quartet. He took the finale for the last scene of the play, with the duel between Hamlet and Laertes, the queen’s collapse and Hamlet’s death.
cues.evidence: Schering’s Hamlet programme for the seven movements, as summarised by Giovanni Biamonti (Catalogo cronologico e tematico, Turin, 1968) at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/.

cues.title: Three closing C♯ major chords
cues.text: E♯ turns the final tonic chord into C♯ major. After the last violin leap, the quartet plays three separate chords, fortissimo. The players stop together under the final fermata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 158, final system: E♯, ff and three closing C♯-major chords. The cue retains the established closing passage time.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From C♯ octaves to D major
transitions.to: B · Allegro molto vivace in D major
transitions.how: The four lines of the fugue converge on quiet C♯ octaves, held under a fermata. The cello then moves up a semitone to D, and the first violin begins a tune in D major. The tempo changes from Adagio to Allegro molto vivace, in 6/8 with two beats to the bar.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke, Serie 6 No. 50, printed p. 122. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus131.pdf

transitions.title: From the D major dance to recitative
transitions.from: B · Allegro molto vivace in D major
transitions.how: The D major dance ends in pianissimo notes and rests. Beethoven adds G♯ to the key signature and changes the metre from 6/8 to common time. Chords separate short phrases, which pass from one violin to the other and then to the viola and cello. The marking is Allegro moderato, and an Adagio follows within this eleven-bar recitative.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 126–127, ending of II and complete III. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus131.pdf

transitions.title: Third movement into the Andante
transitions.to: Theme · A major theme shared by two violins
transitions.how: The first violin plays runs over held chords, and the harmony moves towards A major. At Andante ma non troppo e molto cantabile a new theme begins in 2/4. The two violins share it, and the viola holds an inner line. The cello changes to pizzicato and plays short groups of quavers under the theme.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 127, III–IV join. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus131.pdf

transitions.title: Variations to Presto: cello leads
transitions.from: Theme · A major theme shared by two violins
transitions.to: C · Presto in E major, cello first
transitions.how: The variations end softly in A major, with the lower strings playing pizzicato under a violin note held beneath a fermata. The cello takes up the bow again and begins the E major Presto alone. After its opening figure comes a bar of silence, and then all four players take up the short, quick music in cut time.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 137–138, final A-major chord and cello-led Presto. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus131.pdf

transitions.title: From the Presto into the Adagio
transitions.from: C · Presto in E major, cello first
transitions.to: D · Adagio, G♯ minor, viola opening
transitions.how: After the Presto’s near-bridge passage, ordinary bowing returns and the quartet closes firmly in E major. The viola begins the G♯ minor Adagio, and the other players then enter beneath it. The Presto’s two beats become three slow beats, and the cello joins with sustained notes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 147–148: da capo per l’ordinario, E-major close, attacca and G♯-minor Adagio. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus131.pdf

transitions.title: Violin flourish into C♯ minor
transitions.from: D · Adagio, G♯ minor, viola opening
transitions.to: E · C♯ minor, then major close
transitions.how: The first violin decorates the last phrase of the G♯ minor Adagio while the lower strings sustain its harmony. The key signature loses one sharp. C♯ minor returns at Allegro, in cut time, with a fortissimo C♯ struck in octaves by all four players.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 148, VI–VII join. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus131.pdf

source.title: Beethoven, Op.131 — Breitkopf & Härtel, Beethovens Werke, 1863, plate B.50
source.locator: Printed pp. 119–158, movements I–VII. Two violins, viola and cello, with one player on each part.

timeline.note: The first violin begins alone; second violin, viola and cello join the fugue in turn.
The first violin carries the D-major dance above the other three players.
Short phrases pass down through the quartet before the first violin’s running flourish.
The violins share the A-major song above a sustained viola line and plucked cello notes.
The cello begins the Presto. The first violin takes up the quick tune; later it is bowed near the bridge, which changes its colour.
The viola introduces the G♯-minor Adagio; the first violin carries its last phrase into the finale.
All four players play together, then the first violin plays a melody above repeated offbeats. The quartet ends on C♯-major chords.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Léner String Quartet (string quartet), Jenö Léner (first violin), Joszef Smilovits (second violin), Sándor Roth (viola), Imre Hartman (cello)
fields.note: The item assigns first and second violin; DAHR confirms the four names and instruments. The photographed label uses the spellings Lener, Smilovits, Roth and Hartmann.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original quartet scoring; all seven numbered movements presented in a single joined transfer.
fields.note: The item explicitly presents the complete work in one file. This establishes the intended movement coverage, not a bar-by-bar audit: the performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and any material removed at side joins remain unknown. The public-domain score used for commentary is not identified as the players’ edition.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: These are four session dates for the issued masters, not one continuous performance. AX300–301: 11 February; AX323–328: 21 February; AX332: 22 February; issued AX302 take 4: 25 August. DAHR marks some unissued AX302 dates unconfirmed; that qualification is not attached to its issued take-4 row. The item’s short February/August summary must not erase the two additional February dates in its own side list.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Columbia’s Petty France Studios, London, England
fields.note: The studio is named by the transfer author on the Archive item. The consulted individual DAHR master records independently give London, not the studio.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The item explicitly says the transfer derives from the British issue. The photographed L1581 label reads Columbia Graphophone Co. Limited, London and Made in England.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Columbia (UK) L1581–L1585; corresponding US issue 67021-D–67025-D, Masterworks Set 6
fields.note: Five double-sided 12-inch discs. The Archive description dates both British and US publication to November 1924. DAHR identifies the set as M-6 but notes that pre-CBS pressings may lack the M prefix; M-6 is therefore a discographic identifier, not a claim about the original album’s typography.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 1: AX300-1 — I, first part — 11 February 1924, Side 2: AX301-1 — I, second part — 11 February 1924, Side 3: AX302-4 — II and III — 25 August 1924, Side 4: AX323-3 — IV, first part — 21 February 1924, Side 5: AX324-2 — IV, second part — 21 February 1924, Side 6: AX325-2 — IV, third part — 21 February 1924, Side 7: AX326-1 — IV, fourth part; V, first part — 21 February 1924, Side 8: AX327-2 — V, second part — 21 February 1924, Side 9: AX328-2 — VI; VII, first part — 21 February 1924, Final side: AX332-2 — VII, second part — 22 February 1924
fields.note: All ten matrix/take pairs and session dates agree with the DAHR set listing. Movement-to-side allocation comes from the Archive description, with AX301, AX302 and AX332 individually corroborated by DAHR part titles. The item calls the last entry ‘Side 19’; it is retained here as ‘Final side’, not treated as evidence of nineteen sides. The label photograph establishes AX300 and L1581 but does not make the take suffix legible. No physical run-out inspection or digital join-to-matrix alignment has been made.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The description says ‘My transfer’ and identifies the British source discs, but does not name the transfer engineer. The uploader account and shellackophile-recordings collection are not expanded into a personal mastering credit.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: 27 February 2022 is the item’s added/public date and a digital-file timestamp, not an established date of the analogue transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Ten acoustic-era disc sides joined into one file; Internet Archive VBR MP3 access derivative of an uploaded FLAC.
fields.note: The item describes the acoustic-era recording and continuous presentation; its file list names the FLAC parent of the selected MP3. The photographed label specifies ‘Speed 80’, not a demonstrated playback speed of this transfer. Stylus, equalisation, de-clicking, noise reduction, join edits, speed adjustment and absolute pitch calibration are unestablished. No tuning value is inferred from automatic key estimates, and no portamento or tempo habit is asserted as an audited feature of this performance.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition and the nineteenth-century Breitkopf & Härtel score are public domain.
fields.note: Op. 131 dates from 1826 and was published after Beethoven’s death in 1827. IMSLP identifies the consulted engraving as the 1863 collected edition, plate B.50, and marks it Public Domain. This is not clearance of any unidentified later performing edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: United States public-domain basis: first published in 1924, before the project’s 1926 cutoff.
fields.note: The transfer author expressly dates Columbia L1581–L1585 and US 67021-D–67025-D/Set 6 to November 1924; DAHR corroborates their identity with the 1924 masters, not independently the November publication month. Under the Copyright Office’s stated 95-plus-5-year term for recordings first published in 1923–1946, a 1924 publication has exhausted that term. The Archive metadata supplies no separate Creative Commons recording licence. Admission rests on the historical recording’s US term, not Beethoven’s death, the upload date, an uploader licence or a blanket worldwide clearance. No separate restoration rights claim was identified in the consulted item.

dossier.credit: Ludwig van Beethoven, String Quartet No. 14, Op. 131; Léner String Quartet, London, February and August 1924. Columbia (UK) L1581–L1585; anonymous transfer author, Internet Archive item l-1581-5-beethoven-quartet-op-131. Historical recording: US public-domain publication-term basis.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
